talks.title: Moody's / Team8: Cyber Risk Ratings for Companies
talks.teaser: Explains how Moody's and Team8 are building a cyber risk rating that expresses exposure in financial terms and allows peer benchmarking.
talks.summary:
Moody's, a credit rating agency, treats cyber risk alongside environmental risk as an existential business threat. Its global cyber risk group, formed in 2018, studied how cyber events affect credit. An earlier white paper covering 35 rated sectors flagged 13 of them as high or medium-high risk based on likely financial impact.

The talk covers a joint venture with Team8 to build a standalone cyber risk assessment and rating. Boards and executives want exposure expressed in financial terms and comparable peer benchmarks. The method blends management assessments, surveys, outside-in scanning and inside testing that validates the results, with the aim of completing assessments in weeks rather than months. Three obstacles were described: thin loss data, with only about 4% of roughly 130,000 entries in one commercial set holding enough financial detail; signal decay, where long-standing guidance such as forced password changes no longer predicts resilience; and industrial control environments, which the team has not yet addressed in depth.

Rather than a 0 to 100 score that implies false precision, the team is considering ordinal cohorts that separate firms able to withstand sophisticated attacks from those that can only stop commodity ones. The rating is meant to be transparent and independent, with no remediation work for assessed firms, and the team is seeking community input. Practitioners should weigh the data limits behind any output.

talks.title: Dispel
talks.teaser: Explains how a moving target defense layer and rapid remote access can secure vendor and operator access to industrial control systems.
talks.summary:
This sponsor-stage session looks at how operators and vendors reach equipment at remote industrial sites such as wind farms, solar installations and automated wells. The speaker says that today this usually means waiting for a specialist to arrive, driving someone out to the site, or working through a long login chain. The example walked through a typical vendor path: a VPN into the corporate network, a first jump host, a second jump host for the control cluster, and finally an RDP session. The speaker says this can take 12 to 15 minutes when done by hand, and claims the product connects users in seconds.

The middle of the talk argues that static defences fail because fixed VPN endpoints and jump hosts stay in the same place, so attackers can map them and reuse an exploit once a weakness is published. The proposed alternative is moving target defense, which keeps the path between the two ends changing. The product builds single-use, single-tenant networks across public cloud providers for each session, then tears them down or recycles them afterward. On-site hardware enforces user-specific allowlists. One customer, a water utility, reported about one million dollars in first-year savings from staff time, and the speaker said the security team was no longer seen as the blocker for operations.

The closing part covered authentication, which can either use a built-in console with username, password and multi-factor, or plug into an approval mechanism the organization already uses. For regulated environments, sessions can be screen recorded, livestreamed, or logged through syslog. The speaker asked the audience to bring the approach to their operational technology teams for a briefing and a trial, noting that a discretionary budget could fund it.

talks.title: DHS CISA Director Chris Krebs Keynote
talks.teaser: Outlines the federal cybersecurity agency's priorities, with a focus on its industrial control systems initiative and training resources.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the history of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, a civilian agency created in 2018 from a legacy part of the Department of Homeland Security. The director explains that the agency cannot compel private operators to do anything; its role is to advise, share information and help owners manage their own risk. He lists five disciplines, IT security, control system security, supply chain, insider threat and physical security, and three audiences: security teams, executives and the general public.

Five strategic priorities follow from the period after a 35-day federal shutdown: federal network security, election security, soft target protection, industrial control systems, and supply chain including 5G. Much of the talk covers the industrial control systems initiative, built on four pillars: engaging the community by asking more and giving more, a technology focus that includes the MITRE ICS ATT&CK framework, data integration into a common operating picture, and mapping risk across national critical functions. An interagency working group then gathers industry input on workforce, standards, supply chain and incident response.

The closing section introduces hands-on training environments for oil and gas, pipeline and water facility scenarios, displayed on the conference's third floor and aimed at under-resourced municipal water utilities. Attendees are pointed to the agency's website, regional advisors and an upcoming ICS Joint Working Group event. The takeaway is to engage with federal partners, share what works and use available training to strengthen defenses.

talks.title: Interview with Ed Schweitzer
talks.teaser: Covers designing protective relays, early grid cybersecurity choices, and why power systems demand simplicity and tight latency.
talks.summary:
This mainstage interview opens with the speaker's background as a third-generation inventor and the culture of first principles at his company. He explains that the power industry cannot treat the grid as a lab, so new technology should prove itself with customers who have a real need before standards or mandates lock it in.

He then recounts the first digital protective relay from the early 1980s, which was first sold to a Minnesota utility that used it for fault location. Built-in access levels and alarms were added after it became clear that a serial port with a modem could be abused. Later, customers added dial-back and encrypting modems, and one utility used a relay-controlled phone line so operators could grant time-limited access. He also described how added features and sampled-value designs increase complexity and the risk of misoperations, and he accepted Ethernet ports on relays while objecting to the timing non-determinism they bring.

Toward the end, he asks what inherently safe cyber would look like and challenges his staff to answer it. On legacy code, he says the company rewrites components when it can do them better. For the wider ICS community, he urges a focus on simplicity, low latency and determinism while staying secure, citing a serial encrypting transceiver that added only one byte of latency.

talks.title: 14 Hours And An Electric Grid
talks.teaser: Walks through the first 14 hours of an industrial control system intrusion, from firmware reversing to a rootkit on a serial gateway.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts the first 14 hours of a penetration test against an electric utility's energy management network, where the goal was to reach substation protective relays and disable them. The speaker documented the work hour by hour to give a realistic picture of an average engagement, partly as a counterpoint to press coverage that swung between calling such bugs trivial and calling them reachable only by nation-states.

Early on, the converter's web login and firmware unlock were examined, and its TCP sequence numbers suggested an unusual custom network stack. Reversing the extracted firmware turned up a debug routine that read arbitrary memory and exposed the device password. The firmware checksum was a simple additive sum, so a modified image could be made to pass. The speaker then built an in-memory debugger, carved out a roughly 1.7 kilobyte code cave, and wrote a DNP3 man-in-the-middle implant in C. Spoofing tables kept operators seeing normal values, and compressed truth tables modeled plant start-up states.

Firmware was deployed through an already compromised patch management system. Further exploits against an RTU and an intrusion detection device gave access to the safety half of the switchyard, and the full chain took about three weeks. The speaker argued that such techniques are within reach of many skilled professionals and that actors are often over-credited. The takeaway for vendors is to sign firmware with real cryptography rather than rely on checksums, and for asset owners that legacy ICS problems persist because replacement is never started.

talks.title: Dale Peterson's S4x20 Mini-Keynote
talks.teaser: Urges ICS security practitioners to convince executives to fund bolder, consequence-focused change instead of routine hygiene.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with the history of S4, which began in 2007 to build an ICS security community when fewer than 40 people attended; the event now draws several hundred. The speaker describes a second mission of encouraging creative thinking and dramatic change over incremental progress. He argues the community has largely anticipated attacks: the 2015 Ukraine grid attack used rogue firmware on serial-to-Ethernet gateways, a weakness shown years earlier through unsigned firmware, a spearphishing exercise targeted pipeline companies, and Triton exposed the danger of natively run compiled logic. The core failure, in his view, is not persuading executives to invest.

He criticizes security recommendations from 2010 and 2020 as nearly identical, mostly routine IT practices labeled cyber hygiene, which yield minimal risk reduction for large effort. He sees consequence reduction as a promising idea that saw little progress in 2018 and 2019, and urges trying different strategies. This year's main stage adds sessions on corporate risk management, including board legal duties, a Norsk Hydro loss analysis, cyber insurance, and Moody's new cyber risk rating.

He closes by urging attendees to hold strong positions loosely, meet people they do not know, and use hallway and outdoor conversations where ideas take shape. Since over half the attending companies are hiring ICS security staff, he encourages people to pursue work that makes a real difference.

talks.title: The Future of ICS Security Products ... What You Need To Know
talks.teaser: Sizes up the market for OT security products and how asset inventory, detection and vulnerability tools fit into ICS strategy.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that ICS security has finally drawn executive attention, and that practitioners should use it to reduce real risk instead of producing busy work. Executives often hire enterprise consultants whose metrics, such as PLC patch counts, do little to lower risk, and vendors selling a single bright shiny object can shape leadership's expectations before the security team does. The central message is to set expectations that current tooling is an interim step, because the product landscape will change substantially within two years.

The middle of the talk looks at three promises made by the roughly two dozen OT monitoring vendors: detection, asset inventory and vulnerability management. Passive network monitoring can reveal new devices, but it makes an incomplete inventory. Active queries that use native industrial protocols return richer data, and some vendors now parse engineering project files as well. Passive tools can report missing patches but cannot apply or verify them, so vulnerability management still needs another product. For detection, the speaker argues that passive sensors are only one data source alongside endpoint, firewall, historian and enterprise logs, and that current integrations with SIEMs are largely one-way.

The closing section recommends treating the asset management system as the single source of truth, checking how well each product actually integrates today rather than what its API promises, and expecting consolidation as vendors are acquired or leave the market. Buyers should decide whether to run a separate OT security operations center or integrate with the enterprise one, since most attacks start in the enterprise network. The speaker's final advice is to brief management proactively on the strategy and how it will evolve, so executives do not form their views from other sources.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Detecting Disgruntled Insiders.
talks.summary:
# Overview
This talk discusses a method developed over 15 years to identify disgruntled, at-risk insiders by analyzing organizational communications using psycholinguistic indicators. By evaluating specific linguistic patterns against established baselines, the approach systematically filters massive message volumes down to a manageable fraction requiring review or investigation.

# Key Topics
- Psycholinguistic Filtering: Reducing large corpuses of messages (such as millions of corporate emails) into small, high-risk subsets using baseline metrics.
- Behavioral Indicators: Operationalizing linguistic markers for anger, blame, and victimization.
- Statistical Baseline Modeling: Measuring the mean and standard deviation of specific language variables across relevant peer groups to identify statistical outliers.
- Case Illustration: A real-world example of a system administrator at a New York bank who pushed back against management interventions before taking down critical accounting servers.

# Technical Details
- Baseline & Filtering Funnel: In a client dataset of roughly 63 million messages from 117,000 senders, the filtering process started by querying messages containing more than five instances of the pronoun 'me' based on subgroup mean and standard deviation, immediately dropping the pool to 34,000 messages. Further psycholinguistic filtering cut this to less than 1% of messages from less than 1% of senders.
- Investigation Outcomes: From the final filtered subset, one-third of the flagged communications were referred for a full investigation under the organization's low-threshold criteria, one-third presented issues that warranted ongoing monitoring without triggering immediate investigation, and one-third were false positives.
- Psycholinguistic Variables: The system utilizes around 60 variables, covering dimensions such as anger, financial stress, sexuality, and violence. Key core variables include:
  - Negatives (Anger): Negations such as 'no', 'not', 'never', and contractions with "n't" (e.g., 'won't', 'can't'), signaling negative judgments and frustration.
  - Second-Person Pronouns (Blame): Direct references using 'you' and related personal pronouns, which surge when individuals feel cornered and direct blame externally (e.g., 'until you fire me', 'take orders from you').
  - First-Person Object Pronouns (Victimization): Use of 'me', where the sender portrays themselves as the passive object of actions taken by others (e.g., 'relieve me', 'order me'). While low usage indicates passivity, high usage serves as a strong marker of victimization.
- Domain Filtering: The method actively filters out non-relevant context, such as interpersonal relationship content (by demanding minimum references to employment) and religious phrases (such as references to 'the blood of Christ').

# Takeaways
- Psycholinguistic analysis can detect 95% of at-risk communications across 100% of examined authors in experimental baselines.
- Identifying outliers relative to the mean and standard deviation of peer communications offers an effective, systematic mechanism to drastically reduce noise and uncover severe insider threats before or during destructive actions.

talks.teaser: Traces the Triton safety system incidents, from early controller outages to the August outage that took down about six controllers.
talks.summary:
The talk recounts the Triton safety system incidents at an industrial plant. The first outages in June 2017 hit one emergency shutdown controller, which engineers treated as a possible malfunction. They checked logs and removed the device for a mechanical test without involving the vendor or a cybersecurity review. The speaker calls this a missed chance to find the intruders.

The August 4 outage, on a Friday evening, took down about six controllers across several sensitive process areas, creating a risk of toxic gas release and explosions. Safety alarms began around 7:43 pm, and program-mode warnings were dismissed as routine because they only needed daily acknowledgement. Investigators found Python executables, a Triton trial log and unidentified programs running in controller memory. An engineering system imaged in time still held the tools, because the attackers had left them there; when checked later, the files had been deleted and wiped. Despite a segmented design on paper, weak DMZ firewall configuration let the attacker move from the IT network into the plant network. Antivirus caught Mimikatz activity on the IT side, but those alerts never reached a central SOC.

Each outage kept the plant down for at least a week and brought lost production, product flushing and costly third-party investigation and recovery. The takeaway: when controllers fail, widen the investigation to cybersecurity, preserve evidence, route alerts to a monitored SOC, and harden DMZ firewall rules.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Making Power System Cybersecurity Part of the Engineering Process.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, the speaker discusses bridging the gap between operational power system engineering and cybersecurity by making cyber controls an integral part of the standard engineering, design, testing, and commissioning workflows. Historically, cybersecurity in operational technology (OT) has often been bolted on post-deployment or handled predominantly by back-office IT and compliance bodies unfamiliar with grid operations. To resolve this, working groups within the IEEE Power System Communications and Cybersecurity Committee are establishing standardized frameworks that allow licensed professional engineers and settings engineers to document and test cyber protections directly within engineering schematics and operational processes.

### Key Topics
- **Engineering Design & Standardized Documentation:** Traditional power systems rely on standardized drawings and function codes (such as IEEE PC37.2 relay protection codes like 50, 51, and 87) that clearly define what an intelligent electronic device (IED) or remote terminal unit (RTU) does. The speaker highlights an ongoing IEEE effort to create standard function codes for cybersecurity controls (e.g., local logging, role-based access control, complex passwords, protocol/port enables) directly on operational one-line diagrams.
- **Testing and Commissioning (IEEE P2658):** Standard power system commissioning mandates rigorous point-to-point and end-to-end testing, but cyber controls frequently go unverified in the field. The working group is developing an IEEE guide (IEEE P2658) defining formal procedures for field commissioning, back-office application verification, and decommissioning/disposal of assets.
- **Shifting Responsibility to Field Engineers:** The responsibility for securing edge devices (such as relays, reclosers, and RTUs) must shift away from back-office IT, compliance-focused groups, and threat-intel whack-a-mole approaches back toward the power system, telecommunications, and settings engineers who configure device-native parameters and communication schemes.

### Technical Details
- **IEEE 1686 Compliance:** Modern IEDs built to IEEE 1686 already possess native security capabilities including local event logging, failed login attempt tracking, role-based access control, and password complexity. However, without engineering drawings mandating their configuration, these features often remain unused or unmonitored.
- **Mapping Cyber Controls to Operational Diagrams:** Proposed drawing conventions show function codes—such as C54 for local event logging, C71 for password complexity, C66 for role-based access control, and C60/C68 for specific network service configurations (e.g., HTTP and Telnet). Routing considerations, including data diodes for fault analytics and VLAN segmentation across substation switches, can be explicitly captured.
- **Alarm Integration and Cyber Lockout:** Substations can leverage RTUs as cyber concentrators by mapping cyber events directly into DNP3 points or converting them into syslog messages without overloading bandwidth. The speaker also notes simple mechanical interventions, such as a hardware-based remote lockout switch (estimated at around fifteen dollars) to block incoming control commands during suspected incidents like Ukraine 2015.
- **Field Realities & Application Verification:** A real-world audit revealed that over half of an asset owner's firewalls were misconfigured (which simple ping checks could have caught), and enabled cyber alarms in IEDs failed to route anywhere. Formal application testing in lab environments is necessary to verify performance under constraints, such as identifying dropped packets or limitations when evaluating encryption over protocols like IEC 61850.

### Takeaways
- Cyber controls must be specified on engineering drawings so that if an element is not documented, it is recognized as nonexistent in the design philosophy.
- Establishing clear testing and commissioning procedures creates accountability across design engineers, integrators, and asset owners while providing as-built documentation for troubleshooting and incident response.
- Engineers and industry practitioners are encouraged to participate in open IEEE standards working groups to shape the common technical language and guides governing power system cyber resilience.

talks.title: A 2nd Monitoring Network at Level 0/1
talks.teaser: Explains why sensor-level electrical monitoring can verify control system process health when network data cannot.
talks.summary:
Joe Weiss and Amir open by arguing that the lowest-level control devices, such as sensors, analyzers and actuators on serial, Modbus or fieldbus networks, have no security, authentication or logging. Network monitoring only shows what those devices report, so it cannot confirm whether a sensor or process is healthy. They use the Lion Air crash and the Plum Island black-start diesel concern to show how bad sensor data can drive automation in the wrong direction.

The middle of the talk turns to physics-layer monitoring. The presenter's company taps a small share of I/O signals passively, without touching the SCADA system, and samples electrical characteristics that slower network data drops. In one power generation case, a turbine that would not start, manually or automatically, was traced to a bad temperature sensor within an evening. In another, monitoring kept showing plant conditions after the Windows HMI went down, and a pump problem was found at a separate facility. A building management case and a dam failure caused by sensors pulling out of a wall were also discussed, and a demo showed electrical signatures changing when a sensor moved even though the measured level did not.

The closing argument is that machine learning can learn how readings such as pressure, flow, temperature and motor speed relate through physics, and flag process anomalies in real time. The speakers present this as a complement to network anomaly detection, and stress that engineers, not only IT and OT staff, need to take part in control system security work.

talks.teaser: Presents GE's Digital Ghost platform, which detects, localizes and neutralizes cyberattacks on industrial control systems in real time.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with GE's view of IT and OT convergence, framed around growth and defense. The speakers describe industrial pressures such as safety and productivity, then explain how a digital twin, a live model of an individual asset built from design data and sensor streams, supports early warnings and maintenance planning on jet engines and wind turbines.

The second half introduces Digital Ghost, a real-time active defense platform. It pairs digital twins of plant physics and control logic with live sensor data to separate normal behavior, faults and cyberattacks. Detection flags anomalies using correlations across many sensors, localization identifies compromised sensors despite closed-loop feedback, and neutralization rebuilds their values from trusted ones so operators can keep the plant running. Simulations covering about 600 normal and 900 attack cases reported roughly 99 percent accuracy. A field test on ten gas turbines produced a false positive rate below 1 percent, and a six-sensor reconstruction tracked true values with about 1 percent average error.

The closing section covers planned work with the Department of Energy to extend the approach to renewables, oil and gas, and transmission and distribution. The takeaway for practitioners is that critical infrastructure can add a model-based layer that validates sensor readings and keeps operations running during an intrusion, not just raise alarms.

talks.title: PASTA - Portable Automotive Security Testbed with Adaptability
talks.teaser: Presents PASTA, a portable tabletop automotive testbed with working vehicle controls for studying attacks on in-vehicle networks.
talks.summary:
Toyota researcher Oshi Toyama introduces PASTA, a portable automotive security testbed built so people can study attacks on in-vehicle networks without a real car. He starts with the problem: vehicles were not designed with security in mind, and on older models the OBD-II diagnostic port had no central gateway, so an attacker plugged into it could send messages to ECUs. He cites the Jeep Chrysler remote hack on a running car, which led to a recall of about a million vehicles, as an example of the risk.

The platform is a small tabletop vehicle with steering, wheels, headlights, doors, brakes and hazard lamps, plus a simple simulator in a carrying case whose behavior is shown on three LED panels. Control commands travel as CAN messages through the platform rather than driving the simulator directly. Attack surfaces include the OBD-II port, junction boxes and JTAG ports, and each ECU can be reprogrammed in C. Safety functions are not yet fully implemented, so the speaker demonstrated how messages sent through the OBD-II port can take over the platform's behavior.

The design rests on four ideas: open, safe, adaptable and portable. Users should be able to rewrite CAN message definitions, ECU behavior and message frequencies. The speaker argues that the same principles suit ICS testbeds: match the testbed to the skills it should teach, keep educational versions affordable, use genuine protocols, and publish specifications openly. The project was still ongoing, with the specification and GitHub page not yet public, and questions about price were left unanswered.

talks.teaser: Reports results of an ICS detection challenge where vendors and open-source teams analyzed mining network captures for planted attacks.
talks.summary:
This session reports on a community ICS detection challenge that tests whether products can build asset inventories and spot attacks hidden in real industrial packet captures. The scenario was a mining operation modeled on northern Quebec, built from hundreds of gigabytes of captured traffic with a 130 GB subset used for the detection phase. A third vendor withdrew late, so the organizers gave the captures and a score sheet to two commercial vendors, Dragos and Kaspersky, and an open-source team, with a few days to analyze them. The attack entered through the DMZ, moved through jump hosts and a terminal server to a historian, and reached PLCs, with decoy malware placed in the business network.

Kaspersky presented five incidents from its product, including an exploitation attempt, a downloader's command-and-control traffic, GrayEnergy connections, a suspicious PLC response, and a PLC that stopped after a firmware update. Dragos walked through its platform's zones, timelines and asset context to follow Havoc and GrayEnergy behavior, including a brute-force against NTLM accounts that pivoted across zones. The open-source pair found some activity but missed parts of the chain and produced false positives, such as redundancy traffic mistaken for ARP spoofing. None of the teams fully traced the final step.

The speakers drew several lessons. Many alerts came from unusual but legitimate OT behavior, so analysts need baselines, maintenance schedules and knowledge of device quirks. Scaling to many sites will require correlation and local triage. Neutral, data-driven tests give buyers a better basis for choosing a product than demos alone.

talks.title: The Industrial Radio Project - Hacking Cranes Using SDR
talks.teaser: Shows how researchers found replay and command injection flaws in wireless remote controls for industrial cranes.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Trend Micro research into the wireless remote controls used on cranes and other heavy lifting equipment in construction, ports, mining, utilities and nuclear work. The researchers asked where these systems are used, how they work and what risks they carry. They tested devices from 14 vendors across several regions, most operating in the 400 to 900 MHz range, and found that captured radio commands could be replayed to move real cranes.

To understand the protocols, the team logged SPI traffic between a microcontroller and a sub-GHz radio chip with a logic analyzer, then mapped those operations to register accesses using the chip datasheet. They built an emulator that tracked radio state and linked it to a flow graph so captured traffic could be replayed over the air and compared against physical devices. Findings included command injection, abuse of the emergency stop to cause denial of service, and malicious re-pairing. One vendor obscured its messages with an XOR keyed to a pairing ID, which the team recovered by building a dictionary of possible IDs. They saw no proper authentication or encryption in the devices they examined.

The speaker also described a remote scenario in which a training video revealed a manufacturer, whose documentation explained how dip switches set the operating frequency, and recorded traffic from a public spot without replaying it. Demonstrations on owned equipment, with permission, included a handheld SDR, a wristwatch-sized transmitter and a remote device connected over LTE. The takeaway for operators is to ask vendors whether their equipment is susceptible and to apply patches. Many vendors released fixes, while one declined to patch a discontinued product.

This session is a structured debate on how an asset owner with industrial control systems should organize security monitoring: one enterprise security operations center covering both IT and OT, or a dedicated OT-focused center. The enterprise side argued that most intrusions begin on the IT network before they reach industrial systems, so an OT-only center risks seeing attacks too late. It cited a SANS white paper describing multi-stage ICS attacks, warned that coordination breaks down at handoffs between separate teams, and argued that one team is cheaper to run. It also held that IT staff can learn OT awareness faster than OT staff can pick up IT protocols and malware analysis.

The dedicated OT side countered that a center's value comes from its mission, not its label, and that industrial operations prioritize recovery time and root cause analysis. It said threat collection should focus on the adversaries that target industrial environments, noted that remote vendor access rather than phishing was the main entry path it had seen, and proposed a small, well-trained OT group that stays culturally connected to IT. Dan also noted that hybrid models with OT specialists inside an enterprise center could fit either view. Hands raised before and after the rebuttals shifted very little.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for China As The Most Active Shaper Of The Cybersecurity Space.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Adam Segal explores how China has emerged as the most active shaper of cybersecurity and cyberspace globally. Segal emphasizes that policies originating in Beijing—spanning domestic regulation, technical standards, diplomacy, and foreign infrastructure investment—will fundamentally impact international technology and security ecosystems. Under President Xi Jinping, cybersecurity has been placed at the very top of the national agenda, framed around the core doctrine that modernization and national security cannot exist without digitalization and cybersecurity.

### Key Topics
- **Chinese Strategic Motivations**: China's cyber strategy is driven by three core interests: domestic stability and regime legitimacy (enforced through rigorous censorship, real-name registration, VPN bans, and the Great Firewall); cybersecurity and national security (rooted in a perception of vulnerability to foreign backdoors and reliance on Western vendors like the "eight guardian warriors"); and techno-nationalism (the ambition to transition from "Made in China" to "Invented in China," avoiding the middle-income trap via initiatives like Made in China 2025, massive semiconductor investment, AI leadership plans, and quantum communications).
- **Domestic Regulatory Measures**: Beijing has rolled out sweeping legislative frameworks, including the National Security Law ("secure and controllable" mandates), the Anti-Terrorism Law, and the 2017 Cybersecurity Law. These introduce the designation of Critical Information Infrastructure (CII), requiring mandatory security reviews (potentially involving source code inspection administered via the Ministry of State Security), data localization, and strict mandatory threat information sharing, supplemented by specific action plans for industrial control systems (ICS).
- **International Strategy & Diplomacy**: Internationally, China projects its technical and regulatory standards through the multi-trillion-dollar Belt and Road Initiative across roughly 65 countries. In international diplomacy, China promotes "cyber sovereignty" under the UN Charter rather than Western interpretations of the laws of armed conflict, leading to the breakdown of consensus in forums like the UN Group of Governmental Experts (UN GGE).
- **Key Uncertainties**: Segal highlights three major variables shaping the future: implementation friction and bureaucratic competition among Chinese agencies (e.g., CAC, MIIT, MPS, MSS, PLA); conflicting pressures on globalizing Chinese tech firms (such as Huawei and ZTE) caught between international market expectations and tighter domestic state control; and evolving US policy amid looming trade disputes and Section 301 investigations.

### Technical Details
- **CII Review & Localization**: Critical Information Infrastructure operators face ambiguous designations overseen by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), MIIT, and MPS. Network equipment entering CII is subject to state security reviews, potentially demanding source code access, alongside mandatory in-country data storage.
- **ICS Security Initiatives**: A 2018–2020 action plan specifically addresses industrial control systems, establishing emergency management protocols, domestic standard R&D platforms, and legally mandated threat intelligence sharing to reduce dependence on foreign-serviced systems.
- **Offensive & Deterrent Operations**: Chinese defense analysts conceptualize critical infrastructure cyber operations as deterrent measures against advanced Western Pacific adversaries. Technical incidents highlighted include pre-conflict operational mapping of critical infrastructure and state-level traffic redirection, exemplified by the "Great Cannon" attack that hijacked Baidu ad streams to launch denial-of-service strikes against GitHub.

### Takeaways
- Foreign leverage against Beijing's cyber strategy is limited because policies tie directly to existential regime interests. However, historical precedents (such as the WAPI standard push and Green Dam censorship software) demonstrate that unified resistance from foreign governments and multinational corporations without commercial defections can force policy compromises.
- Escalation risks remain elevated due to the lack of bilateral military-to-military communication—stalled since the 2014 PLA indictments—and absent definitions regarding thresholds for cyber acts of war.
- Potential counter-strategies include building multilateral consensus on cyber norms among allies (e.g., EU and Japan) and demanding strict commercial and regulatory reciprocity against Chinese technology companies operating abroad.

talks.teaser: Compares ICS asset discovery tools on anonymized midstream oil and gas packet captures, scoring devices identified and accuracy.
talks.summary:
This session reviews phase one of an industrial control systems detection challenge, an asset identification exercise in which vendors received offline packet captures from a midstream oil and gas operator. The captures came from 15 locations and were merged into a single stream of about 15 million packets and 800 unique IP addresses. Because the data was heavily anonymized, the organizers found that identifying strings had to be scrubbed across many protocols, not only in IP headers, and that sensitive names hid in places they had not expected.

The competitors had roughly an hour to process the files and were scored on completeness, correctness and timeliness, with extra credit for unique findings. The presenters said the tools were generally strong at identifying major automation suppliers and Rockwell and Cisco products, including serial numbers and models, but they fell off for field devices such as drive controllers and smaller components. One vendor identified fewer devices but with more detail and accuracy, while others produced more entries that appeared to be intelligent guesses. Several tools also exposed clear-text passwords, though no single tool found all of the planted ones, and one caught a program download to a PLC.

The session closed with takeaways for asset owners. Discovery tools can surface devices that owners or integrators have forgotten, and adding configuration files, logs and other data sources could improve results. The scoring model also needed clearer definitions of what counts as an asset. Phase two, which asked tools to detect injected malicious traffic, was scheduled for the following day.

This vendor-led session walks through Nozomi Networks' SCADAguardian, a passive appliance that attaches to an industrial control network through a span port, network tap or virtual machine. It inspects traffic from the physical layer up to the process layer, learns a machine-learning baseline of how each PLC should behave, and adds modules for network visualization, asset inventory, vulnerability management and reporting.

The speakers then use the Industroyer attack, also called Crash Override, to frame the threat. They describe three phases: infection, discovery through passive reading of unencrypted industrial protocols, and an attack built from what was observed, using legitimate protocol commands rather than a specific vulnerability. The recommended defenses are real-time visibility, an accurate asset inventory, and combining signature detection with behavioral analysis, supported by geographically distributed deployments that feed a central operations center.

Three customer cases follow. A one-person operations team at a small Vermont electric utility reclaimed time by mapping its network passively instead of using active scans. A large global utility used passive fingerprinting to build an asset inventory matched against vulnerability data, so it could prioritize firmware risk. A security vendor chose the product for threat detection, where grouping anomalies and signatures into incidents, such as a contractor's laptop appearing on the network, gave quick context. The session closes with examples of subtle anomalies, including timing changes, abnormal setpoints and unfamiliar function codes, and with audience questions about the machine-learning methods.

talks.summary:
### Overview
At the S4 conference main stage, host Dale moderates a panel discussion featuring venture capital investors Patrick (representing ClearSky, a $300 million cybersecurity-focused fund) and Tyler (from Shell Technology Ventures / STV). The discussion examines the surge in venture and angel investment within industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) cybersecurity. While deal flow has rapidly expanded from a few deals a year to dozens, both investors offer a realistic, critical assessment of the crowded market, explaining investment criteria, business hurdles, technology patterns, and long-term exit expectations.

### Key Topics
- **Fund Structures and Investment Theses:** ClearSky operates as a security-focused fund with ties to NextEra Energy (Florida Power and Light), seeking financial ROI while leveraging deep engineering resources to safeguard critical infrastructure. STV operates two capital buckets: one targeting Shell's 'new energies ambition' (future fuels, renewables, mobility over horizon 2 and 3 timelines) and another funding technologies deployed into core operations (such as unconventionals/shale, drilling, and production). STV views industrial cybersecurity as horizontal 'connective tissue' enabling digital transformation, remote operations, and automation.
- **Market Saturation and Lack of Differentiation:** Patrick notes he tracks nearly 30 companies competing with nearly identical architectures: network sniffing via taps, reverse-engineering proprietary ICS protocols, rule/threshold-based analytics, and baseline machine learning alerts. Investors find it difficult to discern true technical leaders when products function more as features rather than comprehensive, defensible platforms.
- **Shift from Fear to Business Value:** Tyler and Patrick advise entrepreneurs to move away from security buzzwords ('threat', 'cyber', 'risk') and address the buyer's operational bottom line. Enterprise buyers and P&L owners invest in cost reduction, operational uptime, and enabling remote field operations rather than buying standalone security boxes.
- **Sales Cycles and Industry Ecosystem:** The ICS domain faces sluggish, highly regulated enterprise sales cycles. Success requires navigating established industrial automation vendors (Honeywell, Schneider Electric, Emerson) and building go-to-market leadership (such as experienced CROs, VP of Sales, and CFOs) rather than relying solely on technical rockstars or threat intelligence backgrounds.
- **Realistic Exit Valuations:** Panelists emphasize that unicorns are unlikely in ICS security. Most startups will experience acquisitions in the $40M–$70M range by dominant IT security platforms or industrial automation suppliers looking to incorporate niche functionality as features.

### Technical Details
- **Network Appliance Limitations:** Both investors caution against relying on standalone proprietary hardware sniffers that decode legacy protocols (e.g., PLCs from 1995), warning that end-user engineers are fatigued by managing numerous disjointed monitoring boxes and consoles.
- **Forward-Looking Architectural Trends:** Investors look for architectures aligned with IT/OT convergence, including containerized applications, Software-Defined Networking (SDN) for flexible control implementation, virtualization, and built-in security for next-generation wireless industrial networks, microgrids, low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite links, and cloud/edge industrial IoT (IIoT) analytics platforms.

### Takeaways
- **Build for Future Infrastructures:** Security must be natively built into emerging technologies (renewables, distributed microgrids, remote automated operations) rather than retrofitting outdated legacy architectures.
- **Address Buyer Economics:** Founders must move beyond 'founderitis,' build strong business teams, partner with key supply-chain automation vendors, and engage decision-makers who hold direct P&L accountability.
- **Expect Strategic Consolidation:** Moderate return expectations (2x–3x) and feature consolidation are standard; successful serial founders use acquisitions as stepping stones for subsequent ventures.

talks.summary:
This closing-panel discussion looks at Triton, the attack on a safety system in an industrial plant, and what the community should take from it. It opens with the vendor response. Schneider Electric's decision to speak openly on stage is presented as real progress, compared with the defensive reaction Siemens gave after Stuxnet in 2010. The speaker, Ralph Langner, argues that the attackers' operational security was poor, and that experimenting on a live target while trying to disable a safety system, which exists to prevent harm to people, makes little sense.

The middle of the talk covers what public accounts still leave out: how the attackers reached the engineering workstation, whether a dropper or command-and-control channel was involved, and what the payload was designed to do. The speaker suggests the payload could be inferred from the physical process a safety controller protects and the actuators wired to it, since a safety controller has a very narrow purpose. He cautions against early nation-state attribution and against overstating the attack before the facts are known. He also notes that basic controls, such as application whitelisting or file integrity monitoring on engineering stations, could have blocked the intrusion.

The closing point concerns legacy infrastructure. The controller involved was about 16 years old, which shows how hard it is to secure installed industrial systems. The panelists encourage practitioners to put replacing aging controllers in front of executives as a serious option, and to expect more detail once the asset owner and investigators share findings.

talks.title: Remote Control Automobiles: Hacking The Snapshot Dongle
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Remote Control Automobiles: Hacking The Snapshot Dongle.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Corey Thune (senior researcher with Digital Bond Labs and former consultant with Southfork Security) explores the intersection of industrial control systems (ICS) and modern automobile security. Emphasizing that modern vehicles are essentially 4,000-pound critical control systems operating on public infrastructure, Thune investigates the security risks introduced when third-party dongles are plugged into vehicles' internal networks to stream telematics and driving data back to corporate networks.

### Key Topics
- **Automotive and ICS Parallels**: Vehicle networks like the Controller Area Network (CAN bus) share significant architectural similarities with traditional ICS and SCADA networks. Both were historically treated as isolated systems and designed without built-in security controls.
- **CAN Bus Vulnerabilities**: CAN bus is an unauthenticated, unencrypted broadcast network. Any device connected to it can send messages to critical safety components such as the engine control unit (ECU), brakes, or steering mechanisms.
- **Third-Party OBD-II Dongles**: Devices like Progressive's Snapshot dongle plug directly into the federally mandated On-Board Diagnostics (OBD-II) port to collect driver data, bridging the vehicle's internal CAN network with external cellular networks (e.g., GPRS).

### Technical Details
Thune conducted a hardware and firmware security assessment of the Progressive Snapshot dongle manufactured by Xirgo Technologies (Zirgo Tech):
- **Hardware Teardown**: The device features a power regulation daughterboard, a CAN transceiver, a CAN bootloader to monitor wake states, an Atmel ARM CPU, an external flash chip, JTAG pads, and an off-the-shelf u-blox cellular daughterboard.
- **Firmware Extraction & Analysis**: Thune extracted the firmware directly by pulling the flash memory chip with assistance from Robert Leale and reading it. Analysis was conducted using `strings` and IDA Pro (leveraging the `eyeball2` plugin by Reid Wightman). Strings revealed internal file paths referencing Minnesota-based development, project codename "ocarina", and underlying FreeRTOS firmware.
- **Cellular & Logic Analysis**: Using a Saleae logic analyzer hooked up to the cellular board's UART interface, Thune monitored the AT commands exchanged between the CPU and cellular modem. The AT commands revealed that cellular network profile configuration lacked proper authentication, and communications utilized unencrypted channels like FTP rather than modern secure protocols.
- **Lack of Defensive Controls**: The device lacked fundamental modern embedded security practices, including firmware signing, secure boot mechanisms, mutual authentication, and encrypted transit.

### Takeaways
Thune concludes that third-party vendors are connecting insecure-by-design internal control networks to the wider internet without adopting foundational security mechanisms developed over the past decade. If an OBD-II dongle or backend carrier infrastructure is compromised, attackers could potentially pivot into the vehicle's CAN bus and issue unauthorized commands affecting vehicle operation. To mitigate these risks, Thune recommends hardware and software isolation—strictly limiting dongle firmware to read-only or constrained diagnostic CAN commands over segregated serial interfaces rather than allowing arbitrary bus communication.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The Great Debate: Anti Virus and Monthly Security Patching Should Be Abandoned In ICS.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This session, titled "The Great Debate," features a structured panel discussion on whether antivirus (AV) and monthly security patching should be abandoned in Industrial Control Systems (ICS). Facilitated by Dale Peterson, the session opens with two opposing advocates: Billy Rios, arguing for maintaining rigorous patching regimens, and Michael, an engineer arguing from an operational availability standpoint against disruptive monthly updates and AV overhead. The floor is then opened to conference attendees, sparking an extensive discussion on operational uptime, risk modeling, testing, and system architecture.

### Key Topics
- **Adversary Relentlessness vs. Operational Stability:** Billy Rios outlines the attacker mindset, emphasizing that offensive researchers and adversaries do not stop seeking opportunities. Drawing on his experience as a former Internet Explorer security program manager, Rios argues that patching is difficult and demanding, but necessary to raise the bar against relentless attackers.
- **Engineering and Availability Constraints:** Michael presents the perspective of critical infrastructure operators (power, water, natural gas), emphasizing that the primary imperative is process reliability and deterministic real-time control. A single untimely reboot or a delay of seconds can disrupt turbines or critical processes, while patches and AV signature updates inherently introduce unquantified operational risks.
- **Vendor Roles and Testing Realities:** Participants discuss the limits of testing. Rios highlights that enterprise software vendors include major applications in test matrices only when demand or risk is severe, urging ICS asset owners to exert pressure on vendors. Others note that industrial systems are often semi-custom implementations, complicating vendor guarantees.
- **Partial Patching and Risk Management:** The room debates realistic patching practices, such as patching only operating systems or applying updates quarterly or semi-annually. Commentators note that decisions are rarely binary; asset owners must weigh business risk, process interruption costs, and compensating controls.
- **Antivirus Inefficiencies and Contractor Auditing:** Multiple speakers note AV's weaknesses, including its vulnerability to polymorphic code and inability to stop targeted penetration testing. Ralph Langner shares observations that roughly half of his clients experienced malware outbreaks despite having AV installed, emphasizing that lack of policy enforcement and auditing—particularly regarding third-party contractor laptops—undermines basic defenses.

### Technical Details
- **Reboot Risks and Latency:** The debate notes Ralph Langner’s observation that 21 seconds of disruption could impair sensitive industrial processes like uranium enrichment, illustrating why unexpected reboots and AV scan latency during alarm storms present direct physical hazards.
- **System Hardening vs. Bloat:** Speakers point out that deterministic ICS environments should minimize attack surfaces by removing unnecessary software and hardening systems rather than relying purely on stacked defensive agents like AV and whitelisting.
- **Alternative Patching Paradigms:** Attendees explore academic and engineering solutions, such as employing formal mathematical methods to verify patch safety without requiring reboots, as well as leveraging virtualization to enable rapid rollback of faulty updates.

### Takeaways
Informal votes taken at the conclusion show that while many participants recognize AV is technically dated and limited against advanced threats, the vast majority still rely on it to catch low-hanging automated malware and USB-borne threats. Similarly, attendees overwhelmingly reject completely abandoning security patching, agreeing that while monthly cycles may be unfeasible for 24/7 continuous operations, patching remain an essential risk-reduction practice when combined with testing, architecture redesign, and compensating controls.

talks.title: The Antikernel
talks.teaser: Presents a hardware-based operating system design that removes all privileged code from the processor.
talks.summary:
Andrew Zonenberg argues that conventional kernels give broad privilege to code that rarely needs it. He walks through monolithic kernels, microkernels and separation kernels, then describes the 1990s MIT exokernel, which was built for performance by separating resource protection from abstraction. Moving non-security functions out of the privileged mode shrinks the trusted base and the attack surface, which he presents as the starting point for his design.

The proposed anti-kernel is a set of independent hardware state machines with no software running in privileged mode. Thread scheduling is a simple hardware round-robin queue, and communication between components runs over two on-chip packet networks: one for remote procedure calls and interrupts, and one for DMA and bulk data. Source addresses are stamped by a formally verified transceiver, and routing is hardwired, so access can be controlled by message origin. A hardware allocator hands out physical memory pages, and protection is enforced when a page is actually accessed rather than when it is mapped. A hardware ELF loader can also check signatures on program headers before a process starts.

The prototype runs on an FPGA, with a critical core of under ten thousand lines and the network and parts of the name server covered by formal correctness proofs. Speed has not been optimized, and future work includes moving to RISC-V, adding peripherals, and writing an SDK. The main takeaway is that the design targets critical systems such as medical and avionics devices, where isolation and fault tolerance matter more than raw performance, and that each component's trusted base depends on which resources it chooses to rely on.

talks.summary:
Chris from Meta Mythic and Lisa from Arizona Public Service present their initiative to transform cybersecurity training through applied fiction—a methodology that makes learners the heroes of interactive narratives rather than passive recipients of compliance content.

**The Problem:** Arizona Public Service faced regulatory pressure from NERC CIP grid regulations to train 2,000 employees in cybersecurity for the first time. Traditional training methods—binders of procedures, 40-50 slide PowerPoint presentations, and 10-question quizzes—produced severe disengagement: 36% actively disengaged (intentionally avoiding training), 60% not engaged (clicking through minimized windows), and only 4% genuinely engaged.

**The Core Insight:** Humans are integral parts of security systems and require meaningful development, not dismissal as "stupid users." The speakers advocate upgrading the "wetware" (human knowledge) alongside technological improvements, drawing on the timeless power of storytelling—fables and parables have taught truth for centuries through fictional narratives.

**Applied Fiction Methodology:** The approach preserves three critical training elements: an instructor presence, immersive learning environment, and real-world simulation. Security professionals become the "sage" (Obi-Wan Kenobi figure) enabling employees as "heroes" (Luke Skywalker). Fictional enemy characters represent attack vectors blended with actual security threats.

**Technical Implementation:** Training opens with an immersive security checkpoint scenario (quarantine/access denial) immediately capturing attention. Employees personalize experiences by selecting call signs and choosing facilities to defend (substations, plants, control centers). They encounter approximately 12 attack scenarios—both physical (badge readers, eye scanners, body sensors) and cyber (USB drives, firewall packet inspection)—explained through narrative and humor. Learning occurs across 40+ decision points with point accumulation. Crucially, no pass/fail threshold was imposed, removing fear barriers and enabling continuous reinforcement based on detailed performance data by employee group and location.

**Results:** After training 1,800 employees, engagement metrics dramatically shifted: disengaged dropped to 4%, not engaged to 13%, and engaged reached 83%—far exceeding the speaker's initial 40% target. Employees voluntarily adopted the "defender" identity, reporting it as the best training they'd experienced. Even senior executives sent unsolicited positive messages.

**Takeaways:** The speakers emphasize three lessons: (1) systems include people—upgrade human knowledge as rigorously as technology; (2) storytelling is inherently human and proven effective for learning; and (3) security professionals must enable employees as heroes, not lecture them as failures. They invite listeners to join "the learning rebellion" and offer free access to training samples online.

talks.title: Securing ICS in an IIoT World ... The Simple Solution
talks.teaser: Proposes a four-step framework for letting cloud vendors access ICS remotely without exposing the process to unacceptable risk.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that broad terms such as industrial IoT, and the NIST definition of a cyber incident, have grown so inclusive that they stop being useful for deciding how to protect control systems. The speaker argues that ICS should be secured by context, since a nuclear plant, a chewing gum factory and a small water utility with two IT staff need very different approaches. The focus is traditional SCADA and PLC control linked to cloud services.

Predictive maintenance can usually be delivered through a one-way device, but vendors increasingly want remote operations and engineering access. In one anonymized case, negotiations stretched over more than ten calls across a year before data sharing was agreed. The proposed approach has four steps. First, the vendor defines granular remote services and the owner judges the impact if that provider were compromised. Second, a perimeter device with deep packet inspection enforces only those approved actions. Third, that device is tested, ideally through vendor test reports. Fourth, allowed traffic is fuzz-style tested against PLCs and engineering workstations to confirm nothing crashes or misbehaves. Process safeguards, such as a physical switch that must be flipped before a remote command takes effect, can further limit the impact.

The closing warning is that ICS has repeatedly been connected first and secured later, as happened with corporate networks, Windows and virtualization, and unrestricted vendor access is hard to pull back. Owners should define services and their consequences before opening a connection.

talks.title: Cyber Physical Attack Engineering
talks.teaser: Presents a methodology for finding digital inputs that cause direct harmful effects in industrial plants.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from Stuxnet and argues that its real novelty was not its zero-days but its aim at the physical process rather than the control system itself. The speaker contrasts this with typical ICS intrusions, where an attacker gains control of a controller or HMI without a clear route to physical damage. He defines cyber physical attack engineering as applying technical analysis and experiments to identify digital attacks that produce harmful physical effects.

He then walks through the attack surface from the outside in. Taking over an HMI, abusing proprietary engineering interfaces that lack authentication, and sending Modbus commands usually offer limited physical risk because protection logic still blocks harmful actions. Manipulating control, protection or safety logic is far more serious, and so is tampering with sensors, since spoofed or miscalibrated readings can keep overpressure valves from opening while the legitimate logic keeps running. Stuxnet's overpressure and rotor speed vectors serve as the main examples. He also groups physical outcomes into catastrophic destruction, mass casualties through hazardous material release, equipment degradation, and product compromise, and suggests process transients and support systems such as lubrication as useful waypoints.

He closes by framing the problem as a maze from cyber entry points to physical exits, where defenders can find and cut viable paths. Existing safety analyses are a starting point, but they must be extended to cover malicious compromise. He argues that contractor laptops deserve more attention than they usually get, and he calls for a shared taxonomy and methodology. The main takeaway is that concrete, process-level risk findings are more likely to win the attention of asset owners and boards.

He also borrows the police use-of-force continuum, arguing that responses to drones should escalate from detection to video monitoring to active mitigation, with each higher step demanding more cost and effort. He scored 25 drones using his own weightings, grouping them from ones he does not care about to ones he does.

He closes with forensics. Pulling logs from a DJI drone by powering it on in read-write mode is poor practice, and evidence that may reach a court needs forensically safe tooling. Because each vendor's log format must be reverse engineered, he calls for community tools. He shares his threat models for others to edit and urges organizations to build their own threat lists and response options through repeated internal discussion.

talks.title: The Key Role of EPC's in Industrial Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The Key Role of EPC's in Industrial Cybersecurity.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In mega-projects across oil, gas, water desalination, and critical infrastructure, Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) companies play an indispensable role. These firms execute massive, multi-billion-dollar turnkey projects over 6 to 9 years. While asset owners increasingly require cybersecurity at the conceptual phase, EPCs often lack the core competencies needed to properly interpret, design, and implement these requirements. Using an analogy to "The Good, the Bad and the Ugly," the speaker highlights that cybersecurity across critical infrastructure fails not from bad intent, but from misaligned incentives, complex multi-tier supply chains, and a severe capability gap.

### Key Topics
- **The Structure of Industrial Mega-Projects**: Projects typically span 6–9 years across conceptual design, front-end engineering, detailed engineering, procurement, construction, and extensive testing (FAT, IFAT, SAT). While 64% face cost overruns and 73% experience schedule delays, cybersecurity represents a miniscule fraction of the total project budget despite carrying critical operational and safety risks.
- **Challenges Faced by EPCs**: EPCs typically operate under lump-sum (fixed-price) contracts with compressed schedules. While they have deep expertise in automation, piping, and physical safety, they struggle with IT/OT convergence, lack internal cybersecurity skills, and face difficulty differentiating between cybersecurity service providers.
- **Supply Chain and Subcontractor Realities**: A single oil and gas mega-project may encompass ~70 main systems (e.g., ICSS, power management, telecom, ancillary systems) from roughly 20 industrial vendors. While four or five large vendors have developed mature industrial cybersecurity capabilities, many smaller tier-2/3 component vendors lack any dedicated security personnel and cannot comprehend or address risk assessment findings.
- **The Scope Gap and Financial Friction**: EPCs frequently sign fixed-price contracts agreeing to broad owner security requirements without fully understanding the technical or cost implications. Years into the project—sometimes as late as year six—an independent security review reveals massive deviations between what was requested and what was built, triggering costly scope expansions, contract renegotiations, and project delays.

### Technical Details
- **Project Scale Example**: Based on a real-world $3.5B project spanning 8 years: over 4 million engineering man-hours, 50,000+ design drawings, 20 million construction man-hours, 66,000 tons of infrastructure, 250 km of piping, and 225 km of cabling.
- **Cybersecurity Review Scope**: Across ~70 industrial systems, cybersecurity reviews involved vetting over 1,000 IP addresses and more than 600 technical documents totaling over 220,000 pages.
- **Testing & Verification**: Security validation must span architecture reviews, risk assessments, Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT), Integrated FAT (IFAT), and Site Acceptance Testing (SAT).

### Takeaways
- **Build Internal EPC Capabilities**: EPCs must develop in-house industrial cybersecurity skill sets and integrate them directly into existing discipline teams (process safety, instrumentation, and automation).
- **Dedicated Project Security Roles**: Projects must designate a permanent industrial cybersecurity lead/role from day one to maintain end-to-end accountability across procurement and vendor management.
- **Form Cybersecurity Working Groups**: Asset owners, EPCs, and industrial vendors must establish joint cybersecurity committees early in the project lifecycle rather than meeting years into construction.
- **Engage Independent Trusted Advisors**: Similar to Project Management Consultants (PMCs), engaging an independent industrial cybersecurity trusted contractor helps bridge gaps across complex supply chains and oversee lifecycle compliance.

talks.title: Interview with Justine Bone of MedSec on St. Jude Disclosures / Short Selling
talks.teaser: Interview with MedSec's CEO about disclosing St. Jude cardiac device flaws and the unusual short-selling partnership behind it.
talks.summary:
In this S4 main-stage interview, MedSec chief executive Justine Bone discusses research into implantable cardiac devices. Over roughly 18 months the team examined major manufacturers, and St. Jude Medical's products stood out as the least secure. The weaknesses included missing or weak encryption and authentication, poor input validation in the radio protocols between devices, and hardware with easy access to ports and firmware, allowing root privileges to be obtained quickly.

The talk then turns to the unusual disclosure path. MedSec licensed its findings to Muddy Waters, which published a report and announced a short position. Bone explained that earlier reports from other researchers had been ignored, so the team chose a route intended to force accountability. The vendor responded with a lawsuit, while the FDA and DHS later confirmed the issues. St. Jude released an update for the home monitoring unit, but the implants remained unpatched, and a battery recall left patients weighing whether to disconnect their monitors. On the ethics of profit, Bone said cost recovery is acceptable, but funding research this way is not something to encourage.

The closing part looks ahead. Future implant firmware updates will need clear answers about who may deploy code and how it is verified, since the research showed that commands could be sent by an attacker. Bone's stated goals were holding the manufacturer accountable and giving patients the information needed to discuss risks with their doctors.

talks.teaser: Introduces Project Basecamp, a multi-researcher study of popular PLCs and the Metasploit and scanner tools released from it.
talks.summary:
This session opens a longer presentation on Project Basecamp, a research effort that grew out of a Black Hat talk on Siemens S7 PLCs and a press panel where experts agreed that PLC weaknesses were widely known but rarely addressed. The speaker compares the situation to the early web, when session cookie hijacking was documented for years until the Firesheep tool made it trivial and vendors moved to HTTPS by default. The project aimed to create a similar wake-up moment for PLC security.

Six researchers each received at least one PLC, drawn from the lab or donated, from widely used vendors including GE, Schneider's Modicon and Quantum, Rockwell Automation and SEL. They were asked to test attack categories informed by past vulnerabilities, such as custom firmware upload, and results were marked red for easily exploitable issues, yellow for harder ones, and green where attempts failed. GE devices fared worst, Schneider Quantum came a close second, and SEL devices showed no red findings.

To put the work in practitioners' hands, the team partnered with Rapid7 on Metasploit modules, with the first one for GE D20 password retrieval being released the same day, and with Tenable on Nessus plugins for SCADA devices plus a passive scanner that flags default credentials. The speaker presents the project as an early step, with the technical details to be covered by the lead researcher.

talks.title: Serial Killers: Ethernet/Serial Gateways Exposed
talks.teaser: Surveys security flaws in serial-to-Ethernet converters from Moxa, Lantronix, Grid Connect and Digi used across industrial networks.
talks.summary:
Serial-to-Ethernet converters link older serial equipment to IP networks in power plants, oil and gas facilities, point-of-sale systems and other settings. The talk explains why these gateways matter after a 2015 attack on a Ukrainian electric utility, in which converters were bricked and power restoration was slowed. The research tested devices from Moxa, Lantronix, Grid Connect and Digi in mid-2015, starting with a teardown of the Moxa hardware.

For Moxa, the custom processor and proprietary management protocols on UDP 4800 and TCP 4900 were the main concern. Some models let an unauthenticated user retrieve the administrator password and SNMP credentials, and a single oversized web request could crash the device. Lantronix and Grid Connect shared an OEM chip, and their default four-digit configuration password could be guessed without brute-force protection. Their firmware was unsigned, so modified images could be loaded. Digi's 1SP device allowed easy debug access and crashed on a malformed TCP header, and its Windows configuration tool had a buffer overflow triggered by an inflated length field.

Vendor responses were thin. Moxa promised fixes that did not arrive in the stated timeframe, and Digi said it would not fix issues in that older product. The speaker's main takeaway is that proprietary management protocols are the biggest risk. Reverse-engineered protocol structure can support intrusion detection signatures, and blocking management ports at the perimeter plus monitoring traffic to them are practical defenses. The talk also noted that converters without firmware verification could serve as persistence points for an attacker.

talks.title: Attacking The Plant Through WirelessHART
talks.teaser: Shows how weak key handling and exposed debug ports let attackers join, spoof and sniff WirelessHART plant networks.
talks.summary:
The talk presents three months of research into how WirelessHART is implemented in process control plants, covering transmitters, gateways and network managers from several suppliers. The attack surface runs from field devices through gateways to the plant network and the control systems. Scenarios included impersonating a gateway and manipulating process values; supply chain attacks were out of scope.

The protocol walkthrough explained the join phase, where a device needs a network ID and join key before the gateway hands out the session and network keys. Join keys could come from default values published in vendor manuals, from firmware dumps, or from decrypting a captured join exchange. All transmitters tested used the same vendor system-on-chip with JTAG and on-chip debugging enabled, so firmware could be dumped. The team had pinpointed where the join key sits in firmware but had not yet extracted it. The data link layer only authenticates, while the network layer uses AES-128 CCM* encryption. A dissector was built by extending an existing Zigbee framework. In the lab, cloning a transmitter's identifiers let a device rejoin as an existing one, while a race to displace a live device was only partly tested.

The conclusions were that the protocol is well designed but its implementation has weaknesses, and that a compromised gateway would be severe, including loss of process visibility. Recommendations included physical security, regular key changes, access lists where supported, and key management checks during commissioning and maintenance. The presenters said vendors were receptive to cooperating on fixes.

talks.title: Defense Will Win (In ICS / SCADA Security)
talks.teaser: Argues that defenders can win against attackers in industrial control system conflicts by changing how success is measured.
talks.summary:
A common claim in cyber conflict holds that offense always wins, because an attacker needs only one success while defenders must succeed every time. The speaker argues this runs against history, where defense has repeatedly taken over in new arenas, from trench warfare in World War I to early air power. Industrial control defenders also hold natural advantages: they know their process better than attackers and can change systems without breaking in.

The central problem, in his view, is how success is defined. Today any impact on a control system, even a brief outage or a minor incident at a small water facility, is treated as an attacker win. He proposes asking whether an attack caused an unacceptable impact instead. Cases used to illustrate this include a one to six hour Ukrainian grid outage affecting about 230,000 people, which was costly but not catastrophic, and Stuxnet, which damaged centrifuges at Natanz in a way comparable to bombing. He also cites fraud thresholds and data breach prosecution rates as examples of accepted harm.

His recommendations cover three areas: cyber maintenance, meaning patching, inventory and manageable change rather than deploying technology that cannot be maintained; protection layers that attackers cannot reach, such as separate safety systems or a vibration trip on a turbine; and recovery time objectives that management accepts. In the Q&A, he noted that asset owners are adding requirements to vendors, and an anecdote about a national red team showed that basic hardening blocked it from reaching its objective.

talks.title: ICS Security Assessment Methodology, Tools & Tips
talks.teaser: Walks through scanning and testing tools and a methodology for assessing live industrial control systems without disrupting operations.
talks.summary:
This owner-operator assessment talk explains how to evaluate an industrial control system for good security practice and known vulnerabilities, rather than searching for zero-days. The speaker argues that online scanning is only one part of the work, alongside architecture and configuration review, policy checks and interviews with operations staff. Findings should be ranked by impact and efficient risk reduction, so a fragile single point of failure or an exposed DMZ system may matter more than an unpatched panel far from the network edge.

The middle section focuses on scanning without causing unacceptable impact. Where possible, test a lab or staging system first; otherwise use redundant units, pick quiet periods, and agree with operations which components can go down and how they would be recovered. Two examples show the risk: a port scan hit a firmware-upload port on a safety PLC and left it without working firmware, and a scan crashed a real-time server while its standby survived. For enumeration, nmap with protocol-specific NSE scripts sends legitimate commands to identify devices, versions and locations. Nessus is the main broad scanner, and the speaker recommends credentialed scans, learning the product's hidden settings, and custom compliance audit files. Metasploit and similar tools are used to verify findings or demonstrate exploits.

The closing advice is about follow-through. Look at the root cause of missing patches rather than just the list, prioritize patching for exposed systems, and patch everything at least yearly. Set recovery time objectives and test them, and remove single points of failure.
